title: Tech deep dive: overload protection / error semantics (Hosted vs Dedicated)
next_steps: Redwood to share draft overload error taxonomy + HTTP mapping doc excerpt (Hosted + OpenAI-compat) and confirm final error codes/headers.
HelioPay to share current client retry policy (max retries, timeouts, streaming reconnect behavior) and their acceptable failure modes per endpoint.
Redwood to propose recommended backoff/jitter defaults and a “retry guidance” snippet for HelioPay’s SDK integration.
Schedule follow-up to cover Dedicated capacity behavior (autoscaling limits, predictable shedding) and run through a spike game-day scenario.
transcript:
Meeting: Tech deep dive: overload protection / error semantics (Hosted vs Dedicated)
Recorded: 2025-11-07 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 54 minutes

Attendees
- Redwood Inference: Henry Cho, Brian Murphy, Amara Diallo, Mina Haddad
- HelioPay: Priya Desai, Markus Nguyen, Elena Torres, Jonah Kim

---
Summary (auto-generated)
HelioPay walked Redwood through their bursty traffic patterns (step-function spikes, long-prompt load from batch reconciliation) and pain with ambiguous 5xx/timeouts. Redwood explained the upcoming Hosted overload protection rollout: layered admission control + circuit breakers + deterministic load shedding. Discussion focused on customer-visible behavior (429 vs 503), Redwood-specific error codes, Retry-After guidance, avoiding retry storms, streaming edge cases, and how Dedicated differs (predictability, isolation, SLA expectations, and shed behavior).

Topics (auto-generated)
1) What “overload” means in Redwood vs internal failure
2) Error semantics: HTTP codes, Redwood error codes, body shape, headers
3) Retry guidance: Retry-After, exponential backoff + jitter, max retries
4) Streaming behavior under overload
5) Hosted vs Dedicated: fairness, isolation, burst capacity, autoscaling, and what gets shed

Action items (auto-generated)
- Henry Cho: send HelioPay the current draft of overload error codes + Retry-After guidance and confirm OpenAI-compat mapping.
- Brian Murphy: provide a sample error payload for both REST and OpenAI-compatible endpoints.
- Amara Diallo: confirm where the earliest shed point is for streaming requests at the gateway (and what gets logged/traced).
- Priya Desai: share HelioPay’s current retry logic and timeout settings (SDK + edge) and where they see retry loops.

Questions (auto-generated)
- Do 429/503 responses count against billed usage?
- Can clients rely on Retry-After always being present?
- How should streaming clients behave if the connection drops mid-stream?
- For Dedicated, will Redwood ever shed, or only queue/slow?

---
Transcript

[00:00] Henry Cho: Cool. Thanks everyone for joining. This is intended to be pretty technical—overload protection, errors, retry semantics, and like where Hosted differs from Dedicated.

[00:18] Priya Desai: Yep, perfect. Our main ask is: we need predictable behavior when you’re saturated. Right now we see a mix of 500, 502, 503, plus timeouts, and our client goes kinda nuts.

[00:34] Henry Cho: Totally. Before we jump in, quick context check—what’s your traffic profile? You mentioned spikes.

[00:43] Markus Nguyen: Yeah. We have baseline chat support traffic, and then we do like a settlement batch job that triggers a ton of summarization and classification at the top of the hour. It’s like a step function. Also some prompts get huge—like 15k tokens input.

[01:04] Elena Torres: And our infra is tuned for steady state. When we get bursty, we rely on retries. But that becomes a storm if the server is actually overloaded.

[01:18] Brian Murphy: Makes sense. A lot of what we’re doing is separating “you should retry because capacity is temporarily constrained” from “this is an internal error you should alert on.” And making it consistent.

[01:32] Priya Desai: That’s the big thing. Consistency.

[01:39] Henry Cho: Ok. Brian, do you want to start with the error taxonomy? Then Amara can talk about gateway admission control.

[01:47] Brian Murphy: Sure. So, under overload, we want deterministic, customer-actionable responses. The broad shape is: 429 or 503 with a Redwood error code, a stable JSON body, and Retry-After when it’s meaningful.

[02:05] Markus Nguyen: Wait, why both 429 and 503? We’d prefer one.

[02:11] Brian Murphy: Yeah, it’s a fair question. We use 429 primarily when we’re shedding in a way that’s “admission control” / “try later,” especially when the request is rejected early at the edge due to capacity pressure and we know it’s safe to retry. 503 is when the service is unavailable due to capacity exhaustion or a breaker is open for a specific (model, region, tier) and we want to communicate “temporarily unavailable.”

[02:38] Priya Desai: But from client standpoint, both are retryable.

[02:41] Brian Murphy: Generally yes, with backoff and jitter. But we also want to prevent infinite loops. So our guidance will be: honor Retry-After, cap retries, and add jitter. And we’ll include a Redwood-specific error code so you can bucket.

[02:59] Elena Torres: Today, do you send Retry-After on 503?

[03:03] Brian Murphy: Today it’s inconsistent. With this project, we’re standardizing: if we’re shedding for overload and we can provide a reasonable “cooldown,” we include Retry-After. Sometimes it’ll be a small number like 1–3 seconds, sometimes more. If we can’t compute it confidently, we may omit it and you fall back to your client policy.

[03:27] Jonah Kim: From compliance perspective, I just want to confirm: error bodies won’t leak internal state. Like “GPU pool is on fire.”

[03:34] Henry Cho: Right. No sensitive internals. The code is like OVERLOADED or CIRCUIT_OPEN kind of thing. Not machine IDs.

[03:42] Amara Diallo: And request IDs, trace IDs—those are okay and helpful for support. But not internal topology.

[03:51] Markus Nguyen: Can you give examples of error codes? Like what are you thinking.

[03:56] Brian Murphy: The codes are along the lines of: OVERLOAD_ADMISSION_REJECTED, CIRCUIT_BREAKER_OPEN, QUEUE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, RUNTIME_MEMORY_PRESSURE. Names might change slightly, but the idea is: you can tell if it was edge reject vs runtime shed.

[04:18] Priya Desai: And how does that map to the OpenAI compatible endpoint? We use that path.

[04:23] Brian Murphy: Great point. On OpenAI-compat, we preserve an OpenAI-style error object shape, but we include our code in a stable field—think “error.code” being one of our codes, and “error.type” being something like “overload_error.” We also still send Retry-After header.

[04:46] Markus Nguyen: Some OpenAI SDKs ignore Retry-After.

[04:49] Brian Murphy: Yep. That’s why we also document recommended retry behavior, and our SDKs will surface Retry-After explicitly.

[04:58] Henry Cho: Markus, are you using our SDKs or direct HTTP?

[05:02] Markus Nguyen: Direct HTTP today, but we’re open to SDK if it handles these edge cases.

[05:09] Henry Cho: Okay.

[05:11] Amara Diallo: Let me talk about where shedding happens. The goal is to shed as early as possible—at the gateway—when we know the downstream is saturated, so we don’t burn capacity in the routing service or runtime just to time out.

[05:28] Elena Torres: So you’ll do like request classification? per model?

[05:32] Amara Diallo: Exactly. We classify by route/model, region, tier, and also streaming vs non-streaming. Streaming requests are tricky because they hold connections open.

[05:45] Priya Desai: That’s a huge one. We have long streaming sessions.

[05:49] Amara Diallo: Right. So for streaming, the earliest shed point is still at admission—before we start the stream. Once we begin streaming, we try very hard not to cut it off, because that’s a bad UX and can create a reconnect storm. But under extreme pressure, there are cases where downstream backpressure causes disconnects. Part of the project is to make those cases show up as explicit overload reasons in logs and traces so support can correlate.

[06:16] Markus Nguyen: If it disconnects mid-stream, what should we do? Our current client just reconnects immediately.

[06:23] Brian Murphy: That’s the “retry storm” pattern. Guidance we’re converging on is: if a streaming connection drops with an overload-coded error (or you see 429/503 at handshake), backoff with jitter and cap retries. Also, don’t spin up multiple parallel retries for the same user request.

[06:43] Priya Desai: We do have a bug where our edge tries twice, then the service retries, and then the worker retries. It’s like triple retry.

[06:50] Henry Cho: Yeah, classic. We can help you map where to centralize that.

[06:56] Elena Torres: On your side, how do you prevent breaker flapping? Like open/close constantly.

[07:02] Mina Haddad: I can take that. So our breaker model is per (model, region, tier). It’s not global. It looks at signals like queue depth, saturation, error rates, and latency. To prevent flapping, we have hysteresis and cooldowns—meaning once it opens, it stays open for a minimum time, and it only transitions to half-open under controlled conditions. That avoids thrashing.

[07:31] Elena Torres: So half-open is like allowing a small trickle?

[07:34] Mina Haddad: Exactly. We’ll allow a small percentage of traffic to probe recovery. If it fails, it goes back open.

[07:44] Markus Nguyen: Are those thresholds static?

[07:47] Mina Haddad: Defaults by model class and region, with the ability to override. We’re also trying to keep it safe so customers can’t configure something dangerous like infinite fallback loops.

[08:00] Priya Desai: You mentioned tier. Like “free vs paid”?

[08:04] Henry Cho: Yes—customer tier / service tier. Hosted has multi-tenant fairness constraints. Dedicated is different.

[08:12] Priya Desai: Okay, let’s talk about Dedicated, because that’s part of why we’re on this call.

[08:17] Henry Cho: Sure. In Hosted, during overload, we may shed earlier and more aggressively to protect the platform and other tenants. In Dedicated, you have reserved capacity, so the goal is predictability: you should see stable throughput and latency within the envelope of your reserved GPUs and autoscaling settings.

[08:39] Markus Nguyen: But if we exceed that envelope, do you shed or just queue forever?

[08:45] Henry Cho: Neither “forever” ideally. Dedicated will still have bounded queues to prevent memory blowups and tail-latency collapse. So there can be shedding, but it’s more controlled and aligned with your contract and configured policies. Think: you’d get explicit “capacity exceeded” style overload errors rather than random 5xx.

[09:09] Elena Torres: That’s good. Our worst case is queue explosion and then everything times out.

[09:14] Mina Haddad: Right. Queue bounding is a big part of this. Also, if you choose to enable burst capacity or a second region, there can be fallback.

[09:25] Priya Desai: We do want fallback, but we don’t want it to silently change models.

[09:30] Mina Haddad: Totally. Policy can specify allowed fallbacks: same model in another region, or a compatible variant. But we’re adding guardrails so you can’t create loops and you can require explicit opt-in. If no safe fallback, then it fails fast with a clear error.

[09:51] Jonah Kim: For data residency, cross-region fallback might be a no-go.

[09:55] Henry Cho: Understood. You can constrain fallback to a region set.

[10:01] Markus Nguyen: Let’s get concrete. Say we call /v1/chat/completions (OpenAI style). You’re overloaded. What do we get?

[10:10] Brian Murphy: You’d get 429 or 503. Headers: Retry-After: N (seconds) if available; Request-Id; and our standard trace correlation header. Body: an “error” object with message like “Service is temporarily overloaded, please retry” plus code like “circuit_breaker_open” (again, exact capitalization to be finalized). For REST endpoints we also include a top-level “redwood_error_code” field.

[10:44] Markus Nguyen: And can we rely on that code not changing?

[10:47] Brian Murphy: That’s the goal. We treat it as part of our contract.

[10:52] Priya Desai: What about when it’s not overload—like an actual bug.

[10:56] Brian Murphy: Then you get a 5xx, and the code would be different (internal_error) and we do not want you retrying aggressively. Actually for 5xx you might still retry a couple times, but with longer backoff. The key is: overload vs internal will be separated in metrics and in semantics.

[11:18] Elena Torres: Do overload responses count against billing? That matters.

[11:22] Henry Cho: For Hosted, overload-shed requests should not be billed as successful usage. If there’s partial work, we’re still aligning internally, but the direction is: you don’t pay for a request we reject before it runs. For streaming disconnect mid-flight, it depends on whether tokens were produced. But our intent is to be transparent and consistent.

[11:47] Priya Desai: We’d like it documented. People will ask.

[11:50] Henry Cho: Yep, agreed.

[12:00] Amara Diallo: On the gateway side, we also want to avoid the “timeout” failure mode. Timeouts are worst because clients retry immediately and you don’t get a reason code. So we prefer early explicit 429/503.

[12:17] Markus Nguyen: Okay. How do you pick Retry-After? Is it fixed or dynamic?

[12:22] Mina Haddad: It’s based on breaker cooldowns and observed recovery time windows. We’re tuning it. Early versions might be conservative—like 2s, 5s.

[12:34] Elena Torres: If every client retries at 2 seconds, that’s synchronized.

[12:38] Mina Haddad: Exactly, which is why you need jitter. We’ll explicitly recommend jitter and show examples.

[12:46] Brian Murphy: Our suggested algorithm is exponential backoff with full jitter. Something like base 250ms, cap at maybe 10s for interactive, higher for batch. And max attempts maybe 5-ish. But we’ll tailor.

[13:04] Priya Desai: We have two workloads: user-facing chat, and batch. Batch can wait.

[13:09] Henry Cho: Great. For batch, you can obey Retry-After and then back off more. For chat, you might fail faster and show a friendly message.

[13:20] Markus Nguyen: How do we distinguish “try another region” vs “just retry same region”?

[13:25] Mina Haddad: If fallback is enabled and allowed, we can route automatically. If not, we can include a hint in the error—like “fallback_available=false” or “region_constrained=true.” But we’re careful; we don’t want to expose too much and we don’t want clients building brittle logic off hints.

[13:47] Priya Desai: I’d rather you not do magic hints that change.

[13:50] Henry Cho: That’s fair. We’ll keep it minimal.

[14:00] Elena Torres: Observability: will we see metrics in console for shed rate and breaker open time?

[14:06] Henry Cho: Yes. You’ll see 429/503 breakdown by model/region/route. And if you’re Dedicated, you’ll see it for your pool.

[14:15] Amara Diallo: Internally we also track admission decisions. For customers, we expose the outcomes at a high level.

[14:25] Markus Nguyen: Okay, can I ask about long prompts. If we send a 15k input, and you’re overloaded, do you reject based on size too?

[14:34] Amara Diallo: Potentially. There are guardrails: very large prefill requests are expensive and can dominate. Under overload, we might shed “heavy” requests first depending on policy. We’re doing request classification partly to keep fairness.

[14:51] Priya Desai: That’s sensitive. We can’t have random starvation.

[14:55] Mina Haddad: Agreed. Fairness is part of the design. It’s not just “big prompts lose.” It’s more like: maintain overall stability and avoid tail collapse. There may be per-route policies.

[15:10] Elena Torres: Is there any scenario where you return 200 but then the model is degraded? Like lower quality.

[15:17] Henry Cho: We’re not doing “silent quality degradation.” Degradation modes are explicit and opt-in—like fallback model variant. If you don’t allow it, you get an overload error.

[15:31] Priya Desai: Good.

[15:34] Jonah Kim: On the security side: if you do Dedicated in a VPC, does this logic change?

[15:40] Henry Cho: The semantics stay consistent. The location of enforcement changes (private edge vs hosted edge), but the same error contract.

[15:52] Jonah Kim: Ok.

[16:00] Markus Nguyen: Can we go deeper on streaming? We’ve seen disconnects in other providers. Sometimes it’s like the first token takes too long.

[16:09] Amara Diallo: Yeah. Under overload, “time to first token” is the canary. If we see prefill queueing too long, we’d rather reject before starting than accept and stall. For streaming, the ideal is either: (a) immediate 429/503 before stream starts, or (b) a healthy stream. The worst is “accepted but nothing happens for 30 seconds.”

[16:34] Elena Torres: So you’ll have a pre-stream timeout threshold?

[16:37] Amara Diallo: Exactly, bounded by queue depth and scheduling. That’s part of the deterministic shed points.

[16:46] Brian Murphy: And if you get a 503 before stream starts, your client should treat it as retryable, with backoff.

[16:54] Markus Nguyen: If you drop mid-stream, can you send a final error chunk?

[16:59] Amara Diallo: Sometimes yes, sometimes no—depends if the transport is already broken. We don’t want to promise something we can’t always do. But we can log it and correlate it.

[17:14] Priya Desai: That’s fine, but we need guidance.

[17:18] Henry Cho: We’ll provide “if stream disconnects, wait X with jitter, do not reconnect immediately; cap retries; treat repeated disconnects as overload event and surface to user.”

[17:32] Elena Torres: Also, please tell me you’re not going to page yourselves for 429 spikes.

[17:37] Henry Cho: (laughs) Good question. Internally, we’re updating SLO accounting to distinguish overload-protected errors from internal failures. So we don’t want 429 to page like a Sev1, but we do want to track it.

[17:55] Mina Haddad: Exactly. If shedding is happening within expected bounds, it’s not necessarily an incident. If it’s sustained or unexpectedly high, that’s a capacity planning issue.

[18:10] Priya Desai: From our side, we still have an SLO to our customers, so we’ll treat it as degraded service.

[18:16] Henry Cho: Yep. That’s why consistency matters.

[18:25] Markus Nguyen: What about idempotency. If we retry, can we accidentally double charge or get double side effects.

[18:31] Brian Murphy: For inference, typically no side effects, but for your app maybe. We recommend using idempotency keys where possible. Our endpoints support request IDs and you can add your own idempotency key in headers; we can talk specifics.

[18:53] Priya Desai: We do have some downstream logging that counts “attempts” as “requests.” We need to fix that.

[19:00] Elena Torres: Another question: do you classify overload errors separately in status page / comms?

[19:06] Henry Cho: Yes, we have a template for overload events, but also—most of the time we want the system to handle spikes without needing public incident comms.

[19:20] Jonah Kim: For procurement, we’ll want language around “graceful degradation.”

[19:26] Henry Cho: Understood.

[19:30] Markus Nguyen: Can we talk about “Dedicated won’t be impacted by other tenants.” Is that fully true?

[19:36] Henry Cho: Dedicated is isolated in capacity. Control plane is shared, but we protect it. In practice, your inference throughput is isolated. You can still hit limits if you exceed your reserved capacity or if you configure too-small autoscaling/burst.

[19:58] Elena Torres: So overload errors in Dedicated would basically mean “you’re above your committed envelope.”

[20:03] Henry Cho: Correct.

[20:06] Mina Haddad: Also if you enable multi-region Dedicated, you can decide whether to spillover.

[20:14] Priya Desai: For our residency constraints, we likely keep it single region.

[20:19] Mina Haddad: Great, then it’s simpler.

[20:23] Markus Nguyen: Okay. If you’re doing bounded queues, what’s the queuing metric? Requests? tokens? We’ve been burned by “requests” not reflecting token size.

[20:34] Mina Haddad: Good call. We look at queue depth and also token-based signals—prefill cost and decode load. The breaker inputs include more than just request count. But we keep it stable and not too high cardinality.

[20:55] Elena Torres: What do you expose to customers? Like do we see queue depth?

[20:59] Henry Cho: You’ll see derived indicators and latency, error mix, and overload counts. Raw queue internals, maybe limited.

[21:09] Priya Desai: That’s fine.

[21:12] Brian Murphy: One thing we’ve learned is: exposing too many internal signals leads to people building dashboards that don’t correlate. Better to give actionable outcomes.

[21:24] Markus Nguyen: I agree.

[21:26] Henry Cho: Let’s pivot to retry guidance. What are your current settings?

[21:31] Markus Nguyen: Right now: we retry on anything non-200, max 8 retries, immediate for the first two, then exponential. No jitter. Timeout is 30 seconds. For streaming we reconnect immediately.

[21:46] Brian Murphy: Okay—so that would amplify overload. Our recommendation: add jitter, reduce max retries for interactive calls, and for streaming, backoff before reconnecting. Also, avoid retrying on some 4xx that are not overload. For overload-coded 429/503: retry, but not immediately.

[22:08] Priya Desai: If you give Retry-After, should we obey it exactly?

[22:12] Brian Murphy: Obey it as a minimum, then add jitter on top. So if Retry-After=2, you might wait 2s plus random 0–500ms, something like that.

[22:26] Elena Torres: And max elapsed time? Because batch can wait, chat can’t.

[22:31] Henry Cho: Exactly—two different policies.

[22:37] Markus Nguyen: What about 429 being used for quota/rate limit vs overload. We’ve seen both.

[22:44] Brian Murphy: We distinguish via error code. Quota/rate-limit has a different code (like RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED). Overload has overload codes. Same status code, different semantics.

[22:59] Priya Desai: That’s okay as long as we can parse.

[23:02] Brian Murphy: Yep.

[23:05] Jonah Kim: Any risk that your error code field breaks some clients?

[23:10] Brian Murphy: On OpenAI-compat, we add fields in a way that should be ignored by strict clients. But we’re careful—some clients are overly strict. That’s why we’re doing compatibility mapping and SDK improvements.

[23:28] Priya Desai: Okay.

[23:30] Henry Cho: Mina, can you talk about how fallback interacts with breakers? Like if a breaker is open.

[23:36] Mina Haddad: Sure. If breaker is open for a specific model/region/tier, routing can attempt a configured fallback chain. But we cap it—no infinite chains. And we annotate internally which step was taken. If no safe fallback, we fail quickly with the breaker-open overload error.

[23:58] Markus Nguyen: So the error we see would still be “breaker open,” even if fallback attempted and failed?

[24:04] Mina Haddad: Potentially with a message like “no fallback available.” But again, we’ll keep it stable.

[24:12] Elena Torres: Cool.

[24:14] Amara Diallo: Also, when the breaker is open, gateway can shed at the edge so the request never hits routing/runtime.

[24:23] Priya Desai: That’s what we want.

[24:26] Henry Cho: Let’s do a quick scenario: 10x spike at top of hour. What do you want to happen?

[24:34] Priya Desai: For chat: degrade gracefully—some requests can fail fast with clear “retry later.” For batch: it can queue but not explode, and we can retry over minutes.

[24:48] Elena Torres: And we want the system to not take down itself.

[24:52] Henry Cho: Exactly aligned with our goals.

[24:57] Markus Nguyen: If the spike is just in our account, in Hosted, do we affect others? And do others affect us?

[25:06] Henry Cho: In Hosted, there’s fairness. We isolate per-tenant to the extent possible, but it’s shared infra. Dedicated gives you isolation.

[25:17] Priya Desai: That’s why we’re leaning Dedicated eventually, but we need to start Hosted for speed.

[25:23] Henry Cho: Makes sense.

[25:26] Elena Torres: Can you share what kind of incidents this prevents? Like tail latency collapse.

[25:32] Henry Cho: Yeah. Without guardrails: queues grow, GPUs thrash, control plane gets slow, clients retry, and you get cascading failures. With breakers + shedding: we cap queue depth, shed earlier, keep control plane responsive, and keep the system in a stable mode. Customers see explicit overload errors instead of timeouts.

[25:58] Priya Desai: Great.

[26:00] Markus Nguyen: How quickly do breakers open? Like do you wait for p99 to blow up.

[26:06] Mina Haddad: We use leading signals. Queue depth and saturation are early indicators. We try not to wait for p99 to be awful.

[26:19] Elena Torres: Nice.

[26:22] Priya Desai: Is there any chance you return 429 but the request actually succeeded? Like late response.

[26:28] Amara Diallo: No. If we respond at the gateway, we don’t forward it. If it’s forwarded and accepted, you’ll get a normal response.

[26:40] Markus Nguyen: Good.

[26:42] Brian Murphy: There can be race conditions in distributed systems, but we design to avoid “ghost successes.” Request IDs help if you ever suspect duplicates.

[26:56] Priya Desai: Okay.

[27:00] Jonah Kim: For audit: do you log these overload rejections? We need that.

[27:06] Henry Cho: Yes, we log decisions and expose audit logs in enterprise tiers. For Hosted, we have request logs; for Dedicated/Private, we can route to your SIEM.

[27:20] Jonah Kim: Great.

[27:22] Elena Torres: Another question: if we do Dedicated, do we still get 429?

[27:28] Brian Murphy: Potentially. The status code may be the same, but error code would be different, like CAPACITY_EXCEEDED vs platform overload. We’re aligning it so you can reuse client logic.

[27:44] Priya Desai: That’s fine.

[27:47] Markus Nguyen: I want to make sure: 429 due to our own rate limit vs 429 due to your overload—different error codes.

[27:54] Brian Murphy: Correct.

[28:00] Henry Cho: We’re at about halfway. Anything else on semantics before we talk next steps?

[28:06] Priya Desai: I want an explicit recommendation from you for streaming reconnect. Like a snippet.

[28:12] Brian Murphy: Yep. We’ll send something like: on disconnect, wait min(Retry-After, computed backoff) + jitter; limit to N reconnects; if repeated failures, switch to non-streaming or show failure.

[28:29] Markus Nguyen: That’s good.

[28:31] Elena Torres: And can you include “don’t do concurrent retries” like dedupe.

[28:36] Brian Murphy: Yes.

[28:39] Amara Diallo: Also: keepalive and timeouts. If you set your gateway timeouts too low, you create false timeouts and then retry storms.

[28:50] Priya Desai: We have 30 seconds. Maybe too low for first token sometimes.

[28:56] Henry Cho: Depends on model and prompt size. If you have giant prompts, first token might be higher. We can share recommended timeouts for your workloads.

[29:09] Markus Nguyen: Okay.

[29:12] Henry Cho: Competitors you’ve tried—are you seeing similar issues?

[29:16] Priya Desai: Yeah. Bedrock was a bit opaque, Azure gave us throttles but not consistent. Together gave us 5xx under spikes. Fireworks had better docs but we still got weird 502s.

[29:31] Henry Cho: Got it.

[29:34] Mina Haddad: One more nuance: dedicated vs hosted isn’t just isolation, it’s also how we do fairness. Hosted has global policies to avoid starving small tenants; Dedicated is “it’s your pool.”

[29:50] Priya Desai: Makes sense.

[29:53] Elena Torres: Can we get a timeline? When do these overload semantics land.

[29:59] Henry Cho: We’re rolling it out in phases. Some parts already in canary. For customers, we can coordinate so you’re not surprised by new 429 behavior. We’ll communicate and you can test in staging.

[30:15] Priya Desai: Please do. We don’t want to wake up to new behavior.

[30:19] Henry Cho: Yep.

[30:22] Markus Nguyen: If we want to test, can you simulate overload?

[30:27] Henry Cho: Yes. We have perf canaries and we can do a controlled game day in a sandbox environment. For Hosted, we can do it against a test project with rate shaping.

[30:41] Elena Torres: Perfect.

[30:44] Henry Cho: Okay, quick recap of asks I heard: (1) stable error codes and sample payloads, (2) explicit retry/backoff guidance including streaming, (3) clarity on billing behavior for rejected requests, and (4) Dedicated semantics around predictable shedding.

[31:04] Priya Desai: Yep.

[31:06] Henry Cho: Great. We’ll follow up with docs and schedule another call focused on Dedicated capacity envelope.

[31:14] Jonah Kim: And I’ll likely have a security review later, but today’s good.

[31:18] Henry Cho: Great.

[31:20] Markus Nguyen: One last thing: can you ensure your error message is short. Some of our logging truncates.

[31:26] Brian Murphy: Yep. We keep messages short and codes machine-readable.

[31:32] Priya Desai: Awesome.

[31:34] Henry Cho: Okay, let’s go to next steps.
